content: The following studies and trials have been conducted to evaluate the impact of various nutritional interventions on the health and growth of infants and young children: 1. A study in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo, assessed the effectiveness of a soybean-maize-sorghum-based ready-to-use complementary food paste on infant growth. (Am J Clin Nutr, 2012) 2. (Annals of Nutrition & Metabolism, 2017; Yale J Biol Med, 2018) 3. A study in Ghana evaluated the effect of Moringa oleifera-fortified complementary foods on hemoglobin levels and growth in infants, showing positive outcomes. (Food Sci, 2019) 4. Long-term consumption of beef extended with soy protein was studied for its effects on iron status in men, women, and children. (Plant Foods Hum Nutr, 1987) 5. A trial in Cambodia tested the efficacy of locally-produced, micronutrient-fortified ready-to-use supplementary food (RUSF) in preventing growth faltering and improving micronutrient status in children under two years. (Annals of Nutrition & Metabolism, 2017; Nutr J, 2018) 6. The acceptability of locally-produced RUSF for children under two years in Cambodia was evaluated, showing promising results. (Matern Child Nutr, 2019) 7. A randomized controlled trial tested the impact of a multi-nutrient fortified juice on nutritional outcomes. (Boston U, 2008) 8. A double-blind, randomized trial in Morocco demonstrated that iron fortification using NaFeEDTA reduced lead burden and improved iron status in lead-exposed children. (2015) 9. Studies in Burkina Faso and Ghana explored the effects of phytase on zinc absorption from millet-based porridge and the impact of zinc-fortified foods on growth and plasma zinc concentrations. (Eur J Clin Nutr, 2017; Am J Clin Nutr, 2007) 10. Research in Bangladesh examined the role of complementary food supplements in improving dietary nutrient adequacy without replacing home food consumption. (J Nutr, 2018) 11. (Current Developments in Nutrition, 2019) 12. Trials in Brazil assessed the impact of iron-fortified orange juice and drinking water on hemoglobin levels and iron deficiency anemia in preschool children. (Nutrition Research, 2003; Food Nutr Bull, 2005) 13. A study in India evaluated the use of fortified laddoos containing calcium and vitamin D in improving nutritional outcomes in toddlers. (Eur J Clin Nutr, 2011) 14. Research in Pakistan highlighted the effectiveness of home fortification with micronutrient sprinkles in reducing childhood anemia. (2006) 15. A trial in Zambia demonstrated that biofortified maize met the zinc requirements of young children. (J Nutr, 2015) 16. Studies in Ethiopia and Guatemala assessed the acceptability and use of biofortified complementary foods, showing positive community responses. (J Sci Food Agric, 2016; Rev Cient, 2016) 17. Research in Zimbabwe investigated the effects of improved water, sanitation, hygiene, and complementary feeding on environmental enteric dysfunction in children. (PLoS Negl Trop Dis, 2020) 18. A study in Jamaica examined the relationship between nutritional supplementation, stunting, and child development, emphasizing the importance of early interventions. (Lancet, 1989) 19. Trials in Peru and Thailand evaluated the impact of fortified cereals and rice on iron status and growth in infants and preschool children. (Am J Clin Nutr, 2003; 1977) 20. A study in Kenya explored the use of high-nutrition biscuits to increase animal protein intake in the diets of HIV-infected women and their children. (Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism, 2013) These studies collectively highlight the critical role of fortified complementary foods and targeted nutritional interventions in addressing micronutrient deficiencies, improving growth, and enhancing overall health outcomes in vulnerable populations.
